Police Interviews - Babies I-P Submissions regarding the evidence of Eirian Powell

DS DANIELLE STONIER (continued)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY (continued)
Application Submissions by MR MYERS Submissions by MR JOHNSON Reply by MR MYERS
Tuesday, 25 April 2023
(In the absence of the jury)
My Lord, bundle 2 should have made its way -- thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Mr Astbury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, we had reached on the last occasion the final four dividers in bundle 1, which are the interviews concerning [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Before we read those interviews, there was an issue that arose in the interview on [Baby F] and the precise wording used on the tape. It has been checked and we can confirm, so I was going to ask if we can perhaps go back to that page now and everybody make the same amendment.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is page [redacted] and it's behind the divider marked [redacted]. Everyone has page [redacted]?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
It's the second reply down the page, my Lord. It begins:
"We've had a few babies on the unit who have had hyperinsulinaemia, which is what I spoke about before the end."
And then it should say "endocrine condition" as opposed to "a crying condition".
Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm told it sounds very similar on the tape, so simply misheard by the typist.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DS DANIELLE STONIER (continued)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY (continued)
If everyone's made that amendment can we go back, please, to the divider marked [redacted], [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Four interviews, officer, as far as [Baby I] is concerned?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: The first one taking place on 4 July 2018. We can see the times set out. We can see in the body of the interview: Okay. This is a continuation of the interview. I'm going to move on now to [Baby I]. There's a few episode for [Baby I], so just bear with me because some I'm going to read out to you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: The officer then summarised [Baby I]'s birth and the incidents alleged to be suspicious. Then Ms Letby's solicitor said: I think in relation to this baby because there's more than one incident, and to avoid any confusion between incidents...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then one officer interjects: We're just going to stick to the note for this one.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then the other officer says: On 23 August 2015, were you working on this date or did you have cause to go to the NNU, the neonatal unit, on that day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure without looking at the off-duty notes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Was there any way you could jog your memory at all? Is there anything --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: My own personal diary.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right. So your personal diary. Did you -- every time you worked would you put something on your diary?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Without fail?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. So if we go to the notes then, this is for 30 September 2015.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: So who was the designated nurse for [Baby I] at this time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, from reading that, myself.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall if you were caring for any other babies at this time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: In which unit she was being cared for, which nursery was she was being cared for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was nursery 3.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay, you think or you remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I'm fairly certain it was nursery 3 but I'm not 100% sure.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall on this particular day what the clinical position was for [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From -- not from memory, I need to --
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- refer to my notes as well. Just that she was nursed on a hot cot but was still having a low temperature so that hot cot needed to be increased during the day that I was looking after her.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Who fed [Baby I] this time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't recall from memory. I'd have to check the feeding chart but I think mum was present for some of the feeds.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: How do you remember that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember from that specific day but I know mum was very present with [Baby I] a lot of the time. She came in for a lot of her feeds?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you recall if you had any concerns for her at this time at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not at this moment, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: No? Do you recall how she was handling?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: You then go on to say:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The abdomen appears full and slightly distended, soft to touch. [Baby I] straining ++. Bowels have been opened."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember -- do you remember that event?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And my Lord, that tile number is for reference if anyone wants to see the note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not in great detail, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: No? You don't remember who discovered it? Did you discover it, do you remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I remember having a conversation with mum about it, I'm not sure if it was myself that noticed or whether mum highlighted it to me.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Had there been any change to [Baby I]'s care prior to this happening?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I'm aware of, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. You put:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Mum feels it's more distended to yesterday and that [Baby I]'s quiet."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember that conversation with mum?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I remember talking to mum about [Baby I], yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: And that particular conversation about the abdomen more distended?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As prompted by my notes, yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: I don't suppose you remember when mum arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: You said that mum was present for the feeds or some of the feeds?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think, yes. I'd have to check the charts. It would be written. Can I have a look at them?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Yes. So mum was present for the 10 o'clock feed and carried out the feeds...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, this is a continuation not a different line, my mistake.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So mum was present for the 10 o'clock feed and carried out the feed and cares. And then the next feed was the tube feeds. I'm not sure if mum was present or not but I know she was there for the 10 o'clock feed because she gave her a bottle.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And then what? What about the feeds after that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So they're tube feeds. So I've given the tube feeds, but I'm not sure if mum was present or not.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. What times were they?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At 1 o'clock and 4 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. So it was mum at --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mum at 10.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And myself at 1 o'clock and 4 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Via tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: You've noted that, "Appears generally pale". Were you concerned at that point at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. From memory [Baby I] was often paler in colour.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Was often paler in colour?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: So who asked for the review?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Myself from reading the notes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Was there a reason why that was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it -- I think it was because I was discussing with mum that -- that we, that she noticed a change in [Baby I], so I asked the doctors to review her with that in mind.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Do you know which doctors they were?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. And I think they were asked to review in lieu of the hot cot needing to be increased as well.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: And how were you feeling about [Baby I] at that point then? How was she presenting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember being unduly concerned about her.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Lucy Letby, it was summarised, wrote up the relevant observations at 13.36 hours. She believed they occurred some time after [Baby I] opened her bowel at 10 am and before 13.30. The question was asked: Okay. Another activity on the notes that you put in on page 2. The date is 30 September at 19.31. Have you got that one?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: And it's got:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Reviewed by doctors at 15.00 as [Baby I] appeared mottled in colour with distended abdomen and more prominent veins."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember who those doctors were?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it might have been [Dr A], the registrar.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Is this in relation to the review that you asked for in your previous notes, you know when --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, this is an additional review.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay, right. And why was -- so why was that review asked for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because [Baby I] had become more mottled in colour and more distended abdomen.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right, okay. And who discovered this mottled colour?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure if it was myself or not.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right. And when you put previously that you realised that she was pale, "appears generally pale", how soon after can you remember when she became mottled?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The following notes here would read that she became mottled at around 15.00.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: So I'm just asking if you remember when she was pale and how soon after was the mottled highlighted to you [as read]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: You don't? Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But I -- I think mum was there when the doctors were reviewing her because I think mum saw the mottling as well.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Can you describe the mottled colour to us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember [Baby I]'s appearance exactly, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. What was the relevance of the prominent veins?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So when babies' abdomens distend their veins become more prominent because of this distension.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And whereabouts were those veins sort of more prominent?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember exactly. Just on her abdomen. I don't remember where.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. But you said about mum might have been there and noticed the mottle [as read]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: It's purely for the timings, that's all.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think -- was it when I've written the next account at 19.32?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have written that mum was present when reviewed by doctors.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then had left the unit when [Baby I] had a large vomit.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. So that's --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I think the 13.48 entry is referring to:
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: "Mummy is to carry out feeds and cares of the morning feeds."
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: So where you've put, "Reviewed by doctors at 15.00", is that when the doctors came to review or do you think that's when she appeared mottled from the way it's written?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I -- I would read that she became mottled around that time and that's when she was reviewed by the doctors due to that.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right. Okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At 16.30 [Baby I] had a large vomit from the mouth and nose++, suction given. Became apnoeic with bradycardia, desaturation (30s). Help summoned and IPPV (ventilation) given for approximate 3 minutes and 100% oxygen to recover. Doctors were crash called."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How did you become aware of this large vomit, can you remember, at 16.30?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you remember who was present?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you remember just prior to that what you were doing at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you remember who actually put the crash call out at this time on this day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I'm not sure who put the call out.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: No? Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And do you remember how soon the doctors arrived?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: I don't remember exact timings, no?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the wrong way round. It should be:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Question: And do you remember how soon the doctors arrived?"
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't remember exact timings, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: No? Okay.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's wrong again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Do you recall who the doctors were?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Then in summary, Lucy Letby confirmed [Baby I] was moved into nursery 1 for closer observations and because she needed an incubator. She was placed nil by mouth and she, Lucy Letby, continued as her designated nurse: So do you recall when mum left the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Did she leave prior to or after the vomit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I've written -- I don't remember from memory but I've written that she had left the unit when [Baby I] had the vomit, that she was there where the doctors reviewed her at 15.00.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Who discovered the vomit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: If we go to the activity date, timed at 20.26, it starts off with, "Peripheral line sited". Have you got that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: My Lord, I don't think we need to put the tile up for this. It's there if anybody needs it:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "... and 10ml per kilogram saline bolus given. 10% glucose commenced. At 19.30 [Baby I] became apnoeic, abdomen distended ++, confirmed bradycardias, desaturation followed."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Clearly, this is the note being read, officer, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: "SHO in attendance and registrar crash called."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall who the SHO was at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Or who the registrar was who you refer to there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure if the registrar would have still been [Dr A], who was on a day shift.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you remember who discovered this event? I mean do you actually remember this event occurring, Lucy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: You don't? Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Only through prompt of my notes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: So if we move on to the 12th into 13 October, and Lucy Letby confirmed that she had the relevant notes before her: Do you recall this event of 12/13th at all compared to the last event? Is there anything specific about that that day? I'll just lead you through your notes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh yes, sorry. So this is when she was found apnoeic in the cot at night.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: "[Baby I] noted to be pale in the cot by myself at 03.20.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: SN Hudson present."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So who had you taken care from at that time, do you remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From Staff Nurse Hudson.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Lucy Letby confirmed that she'd taken over as [Baby I]'s designated nurse that night after the relevant incident: So do you want to tell us what the clinical position was for [Baby I] at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When I took over her care?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, she'd been found in the cot apnoeic -- well, sort of gasping and required Neopuffing and then intubating.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And is -- why was that care passed to you then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because Staff Nurse Hudson was a junior band 5 nurse that couldn't care for intensive care patients, which [Baby I] had then become.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: In your notes you put, "Noted to be pale". Can you elaborate at all on that? Can you expand any observations at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Some of it. When we went into the nursery, put the light on -- the lights aren't on in the nursery at night and we had put the lights on for something and I noticed -- I looked over at [Baby I] and I noticed she was pale in colour in the cot.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So her face was pale.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you remember what your observations were in relation to handling [Baby I] at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think we went over to her and pulled the covers off her and undid her babygro a little bit so we could see her colour centrally.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: You then put in your notes:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Apnoea alarm in situ and had not sounded."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you give an explanation for that at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the apnoea alarm's are programmed to alarm if a baby hasn't breathed for 20 seconds.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When we found [Baby I], [Baby I] was shallow breathing and gasping, so potentially if she had gasped once every 20 seconds or more then the alarm would not have gone off.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then colleague: When you say "when we discovered her", who were you with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Ashleigh Hudson, who was caring for [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And what cause did you have to go to the nursery?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember. We both went in together for something but I don't remember why we were going into the nursery.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And what treatment had you given to [Baby I] up to that point; can you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On that night?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nothing that I'm aware of.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: You then go on to say that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On examination [Baby I] was centrally white."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What do you mean by that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So when we pulled her babygro away and looked to her body she was white.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. What was your thoughts of what was going on then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That she was collapsing in some way.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Minimal shallow breaths followed by gasping observed."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What does this sort of mean to you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So she was breathing but very shallowly and not very often and then was gasping.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: What action did you take at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, we started to give Neopuff ventilation and called for help.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember actually who called for assistance at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think I started ventilation breaths and Ashleigh called for help but that's just from memory.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember who actually came to assist, how long it took for them to arrive?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't recall exact timings, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay, was there full resus efforts at this time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. I think they were just obtaining an airway.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was then asked about her subsequent notes with the question: What do you mean by stiff in posture?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So she's holding her limbs stiffly. So they have a rigid posture.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Is that a sign of anything to you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It can be that they're in pain.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: And then the question is: Is that a suitable time for us to stop, yeah, or do you wish to...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then Ms Letby's solicitor said: We could do one more thing. I am just thinking, if you're okay to do one more, but there's so much to do tomorrow and I think we said we'd do it now, so we've got about 25 minutes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is this the last one for [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: There's two left.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can we leave it then, please?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: The solicitor then said: Yeah, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then the officers: Okay, that's fine. Is there -- just explain to us the reason why you want to leave it at this moment in time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I just feel that I'm tired and I've gone through a lot at the moment and I want to be clear with the information that I am giving to you and I think that would be better tomorrow.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay, yeah.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then the second officer: Okay, the time is 2 minutes to 9.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And that was the conclusion of that first interview in respect of [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Moving to the second interview, we can see, as has been suggested previously, that this is the next day, 5 July 2018. It begins at 9.43 in the morning. It begins with the officer saying: Okay, we were in the middle of dealing with [Baby I],
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby I]. So I would like now to concentrate on the event that occurred at around 7 o'clock and 7.45 in the morning of 14 October 2015. This is when [Baby I] became bradycardic, requiring intubation and resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Lucy Letby confirmed that she'd been provided with notes: It is -- before we go through these notes, do you remember that particular shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember the clinical position for [Baby I] at that time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Lucy Letby couldn't recall [Baby I]'s handover, which nursery she was in or which staff were on duty in each nursery. She was asked: Okay, if we just move on with these notes, there is a -- you've noted some bruising, discolouration evident on sternum and right side of chest from chest compressions. How were you aware of this, Lucy? Have you got to that point --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: -- in the notes? You have? Yes. Do you remember that, those bruising (sic)?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So when a student nurse does a feed they have to inform someone that they've done it to get a co-signature so I've co-

blocks.text: signed that one and then I believe I may have done this feed for somebody at 6 o'clock.

blocks.text: You've done it for somebody? Is that common practice then to sign on someone's behalf?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I mean I've done the feed but I've done it on behalf of somebody if they've had to leave. Yes, if they have said -- sometimes you go on a break or something and you'd say, well, would you mind feeding my baby for me.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember if that was the case?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't remember it specifically, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And I think you've already said about overnight and the treatment with [Baby P] was a little cautious.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did [Baby O]'s death have any other effect on the treatment of [Baby P]?

blocks.text: That he'd had a septic screen that evening as well and he was started on some antibiotics.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Myself.

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was asked about her nursing note which will be found behind tile 263: Okay so the next entry is:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Observations within normal range, [Baby P] nil by mouth. IV fluids: glucose. Peripheral line: line occluding."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Occluding" it should read.

blocks.text: Oh right, okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "High pressures. NG tube on free drainage. In tube. Abdomen full. Loops visible. Soft to touch."

blocks.text: So he was lying in the incubator undressed, so it's just through visually observing.

blocks.text: Loops aren't something that we want to see.

blocks.text: Right. What's it an indication of, loops?

blocks.text: Yes, so -- I believe.

blocks.text: From the night staff?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The night staff, that's when they had stopped his feeds and placed him nil by mouth due to a distended abdomen and I believe he'd had some large aspirates and air obtained. And I think he'd had a few desaturations as well.

blocks.text: Overnight of the 23rd into the 24th?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yeah.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right. What was the time between you making these observations about his full abdomen and the loops and the ward round and the further observations by the registrar?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um, I think the abdomen being full, I think, was noted from when I took over the care at 8 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. Did you escalate that to anybody?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So from what I remember I mentioned it to -- I think it was the nurse in charge and talked about bleeping the doctors and she said, well, the doctors will be here shortly for the ward round, so wait for the doctors.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Who was that? Do you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. It says here:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Mottled appearance requiring facial oxygen and Neopuff for approximately 1 minute. Abdomen becoming distended."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So was this while the registrar was there; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yeah, from memory it was the registrar that carried out the Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. So what action was taken by yourself at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember. I think I was just supporting him in managing the airway and just assessing him.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Had you taken any action at the point where you realised his abdomen was full and the loops were visible?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just that I'd spoken to another nurse about it and they'd advised me to wait for the ward round because the doctors would be there shortly.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. So at 9 am when [Baby P] had the apnoea, who else was present? There was obviously yourself and the registrar.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember anyone else being there.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And where you've described his abdomen being distended, how was it different from the abdomen being full that you'd recognised earlier?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So a full abdomen can be soft whereas with distended it's more firm --
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and it looks firmer and it feels firmer when it's distended.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And this mottled appearance, Lucy, how did that compare to [Baby P]'s brother?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't recall.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. So what can cause a tummy going from full and soft to distended and hard?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If there's some sort of problem with the bowel or the abdomen, so infections or obstructions.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right. Was he displaying any other symptoms during that time prior to the registrar arriving?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I am aware of, no.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Lucy Letby believed it was [Dr B] who performed the emergency intubation during -- although [Dr A] was also present. A decision was made to keep [Baby P] in nursery 2. She was asked: Okay. So at this point, after what happened the day before, what were you feeling at this point with regards to [Baby P]'s deterioration?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Panicked. I think we were all feeling quite on edge about it.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: The officers moved on to the events timed at 12.28: Okay, so who was present during this further collapse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So from memory I believe [Dr A] was inserting the chest drain at that time and I think [Dr B] was present. There were a lot of people around all the time. I remember it being very chaotic. I was trying to get in with drip stands and to connect medications and things and there were just people everywhere.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: I this -- was this still ongoing from the previous event?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think there were -- there was things and an intervention was being done with him the whole time, an X-ray coming in.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we didn't have the equipment in the nursery so a lot of having to go out and obtain equipment from the other nurseries to bring in.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right. Why wasn't he just moved to nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From memory I think nursery 1 was busy and --
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and it would be an issue having to move other babies and then have to move a sick baby --
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- like [Baby P] into another nursery, so they made the decision that as [Baby R] was already in nursery 2 that we could keep them both in there.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Right, okay. So obviously there are further deteriorations there within the notes. It refers to the transport team arriving and a further collapse shortly after. Were you there at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um, I think I was having a handover or giving part of the handover with the transport team.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I think they were stood to the outside of the nursery at that point.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Parents held [Baby P] as he passed away and spent time with him and sibling. Dressed [Baby P] at their request."

blocks.text: Is that yourself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: "... and taken photos of [Baby P] and [Baby O] together.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Support given to parents and extended family. Time spent on suite. Mum discharged. Parents have gone to Liverpool Women's to be with sibling ([Baby R])."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What were your thoughts at that stage?

blocks.text: It was just devastating for us all and then to have to have them both...

blocks.text: And it says "crying" in brackets: We put them top and tail in the Moses basket so I could take some photos for them.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Who asked you to do that Lucy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The parents.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Were you happy doing that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I wanted -- if that's what they wanted me to do, I wanted to do it. And as I say, they asked me to dress him as well.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Did they ask you because you were his designated nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think so, yes, and I think -- I usually offered, would they like to do, and I believe they said no, no, could I do it for them.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: So was the death of [Baby P] unexpected then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Two in 2 days. Did you do all the memory box stuff and everything?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't think I did any of the hand and footprints.

blocks.text: This was quite later on in the shift so I think I just took the photographs. And then I sustained a needlestick injury whilst dressing [Baby P], so I had to leave to go to A&E. So I don't think I carried out any of the other mementoes.

blocks.text: On a few of the others, you know, we have asked you about your coping mechanism and who you spoke to. This is a particularly traumatic time, isn't it? What was your outlet?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we all spoke -- the staff that were on duty, we all spoke about it at the time and then I remember with this one we also liaised with the transport team and sort of discussed it with them as well at the end of the shift, yeah.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Is there anything else that you want to add, Lucy, about [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: And the interview concluded in respect of [Baby P] at that point.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yeah.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, not that I am aware of, no.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know. He'd had problem with his feeds overnight and his feeds had been stopped.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, whether there was tension on the tubing from the equipment -- I don't know if he was being moved at the same time for X-ray or anything like that or if the tube wasn't secure in the first place.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you recall the tube becoming dislodged, Lucy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Did you dislodge [Baby P]'s tube deliberately --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: -- knowing it would cause him to collapse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Did you do it accidentally?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Lucy, are you responsible for the murder of [Baby P]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The officers summarised the previous interviews concerning [Baby P]: When you worked on the neonatal unit, Lucy, did you have any preferences as to which nursery you wanted to work in?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On a day-to-day basis, do you mean?
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I enjoyed the variety. I did like being in intensive care, but it was nice that we were a unit where you could have babies and have them all the way through. blocks.text: Why did you particularly enjoy working in nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I enjoyed the learning aspect and I think that I am someone that -- I enjoy a fast pace and felt that I could do well in that situation and I really enjoyed learning and carrying on from my experiences at the Women's.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay. And when you weren't working in nursery 1 and you were working in the other nurseries, did that bother you in any way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. Quite often it was nice to see the babies further down the line that we'd looked after previously and have a bit of a break from nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was nice to do other things like bathing them with parents and that, not purely doing ITU. I think it's nice to be able to do feeds with the babies and bottle feeds and bathing and things.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you know Nurse Kathryn Percival-Ward?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: She said that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The only thing that started to worry us about Lucy was the fact that at times she didn't want to be in the outside nurseries looking after babies and she would make her way and help in the intensive care nurseries. I recall being involved in an argument with Lucy when I informed her that she would be working in nursery 3 and she told me she wanted to be in nursery 1. Lucy told me it was boring in the other nurseries and she didn't just want to do the feeds."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall having an argument with Kathryn?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't and I don't recall ever calling my work boring in any capacity.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you recall ever asking her to be in nursery 1 when you'd been allocated nursery 3?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember that specific time. I may have done, I don't know.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: [Dr B] states that whilst [Baby P] was unwell you commented to her that he would not leave here alive and was corrected by [Dr B] as he had good blood readings.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recall saying this comment?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. I don't know why I was -- had a conversation with [Dr B] about a baby not leaving the unit unless they were really sick at the time.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Why did you think that [Baby P] would not leave the NNU alive?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I don't recall saying that so I don't think -- I don't remember saying that unless it was at the point where he was physically ill.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you remember any occasion when you thought that, that he wouldn't be leaving alive?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Once he started to deteriorate, yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: It was suggested to Lucy Letby that Dr Brearey had told her that she should take the weekend off due to the traumatic events. Lucy was asked if she recalled any comment like that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: He said that you refused after [Baby P] and [Baby O] died.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't recall that conversation. I was due to go on annual leave after the triplets so I would have been off work anyway. I don't recall that conversation.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yeah, I think so, yeah.

blocks.text: Is that description or that description that you've given, would that be reflected anywhere in the clinical records or notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That he had blown his tummy up? Yes.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: "So just blew tummy up and had apnoeas, downward spiral."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, so the apnoeas should be documented in my nursing notes and on an apnoea chart.

blocks.text: Okay. And what about the tummy being distended?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Should be as well.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: "Blew tummy up", that will be in the notes as well, would it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it should be in my nursing notes and I believe the doctor was there at the time. I asked him to review [Baby P] so it should be reflected in his documentation as well.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: And why did you send that message to Sophie?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know if it was in response -- did she ask me how they were that day? I am not sure.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yeah.

blocks.text: Why did you suggest that to [Nurse E], that there was a bug on the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Who did you speak to about it, about the bug being on the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure.
blocks.speaker: STONIER

blocks.text: Do you remember who mentioned it to you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.

blocks.text: Is it more a case that that's your own opinion, Lucy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is my own opinion, but it was discussed on the unit and again it was discussed about whether equipment needed to be checked and fluids saved and sent away.

blocks.text: By messaging [Nurse E] that you were worried about there being a bug on the unit, are you suggesting alternative causes for [Baby P]'s death?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Looking at the commentary on relevance, the principles behind which, I suspect, we all are very familiar with, it is far too narrow, of course, to seek to contain relevance within those two issues. And indeed, I just note this. In the comments of Lord Simon of Glaisdale, it's at page 3 of the prosecution's argument, in dark print at the top part, from the case of DPP v Kilbourne, in seeking to articulate how one should deal with this in terms of what is logically probative or disprobative, his Lordship there identifies that the risk of, as he puts it,
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: etymological tautology in going round -- this is at the conclusion of that section -- going round the formulation one might make, but settles for saying that:

blocks.text: "If relevant, evidence is evidence which makes the matter which requires proof more or less probable."
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: A good example of where we could collapse into tautology is to look at the two issues as defined by the prosecution and seek to limit what is relevant by matters that bear directly upon that, but of course there are many issues that go towards that from issues of credibility, to issues as to why the defendant did or wrote things that she did. So it is a rather broader approach than simply defining it by those two issues.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: They don't define relevance, they're ultimate issues, so far as the prosecution is concerned, and when one simply deconstructs the offences.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Turning, therefore, to the matters which the prosecution -- the defence have identified and cross-referring that between both documents, (i), which is Ms Powell's assessment of Lucy Letby as a nurse, there's no issue there. So I can move from that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's (i) on the defence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In fact, the defence points are included within the prosecution note, which is helpful, we're grateful for that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It is helpful.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I can take your Lordship through that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So there is no issue in relation to that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The second matter, which is that Lucy Letby was designated regularly to care for intensive care babies once she had qualified to do so and matters relating to that. There are no contrary submissions by the prosecution, though they question whether it's a fact in issue. The defence observe simply that it is relevant her preponderance, her presence at the time of events, and it's relevant, the defence would say, that she is somebody who was regularly asked to look after the most poorly babies because of her position.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The prosecution don't take issue with that, it's something that Eirian Powell can deal with and therefore, we submit, it's something that we should be entitled to establish with her and
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: the related material, of which there isn't a great deal as it happens.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right. I haven't studied the minutiae of the evidence, but to what extent is there going to be a statistical analysis of the number of babies passing through over the relevant period and the extent to which she, as opposed to any other nurse of her grade, was dealing with intensive care babies? I rather think that that is not evidence that can be adduced. So it's going to be in large part an expression of opinion or impression from the witness rather than based on hard evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm not being critical, I'm just making the comment.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think the point is -- what the prosecution, as I understand it, are saying is: well, in principle, one cannot object to this but it has limited value in the sense that unless one is going to descend to careful statistical analysis, it's going to be very much the witness's view in relation to that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But as I say, I'm not suggesting the prosecution are being reasonable or unreasonable in relation to this, I'm simply probing it in a little more detail.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is a matter of impression, but of course in the case there is a good deal that's put forward as a matter of impression sometimes in terms of practice on the unit by other witnesses. It's not a statistical analysis, but it's a fact that we say is relevant just in considering the number of occasions Ms Letby is looking after children who are intensive care babies or present at that time or her, and I put this neutrally, access to them, that she's something who's bound to have more than somebody who isn't as qualified as she was and at the stage of qualification that she had reached.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So we don't give it the status of some type of actuarial analysis, we simply don't. It is a matter of impression but in this case there are other issues that are matters of impression. It may go to the overall weight to be given to that evidence, but it doesn't, we submit, give a basis for saying there should be no -- it shouldn't be brought out before the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right. I will hear what the prosecution say.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It'll perhaps assist if I deal with the points.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I understand what your point is there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Points 3 and 4 both relate to evidence concerning Dr Brearey and things that he has said to Eirian Powell and her evidence is clear that he has. It's in her statement, we've identified where these matters appear.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: One of them, which is at page 206, my Lord, just in the lower part, next to what's the hole punch in my copy --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- was Dr Brearey's lack of interest in the doctors when it came to looking at who was present at the time of the events that were being considered.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The second matter, which is our point 4, it's at page 207, were his comments about Melanie Taylor or his comment about "Mel being nice". I'll elaborate on that in a moment.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Both of these are matters that the prosecution object to and they do so primarily on the basis that they are insufficiently relevant and that the question of bias or confirmation bias isn't something which justifies the introduction of them. That's at the first part of their argument.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We submit -- in fact, we can strip away the word "confirmation" at this point. The question of bias or credibility is important in fact. It's important, we submit, both in terms of how doctors, in particular on this unit, have interpreted events at the time they took place and also how they have approached their evidence before the jury now and matters that cast light upon that are relevant.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Taking both of those, when we talk about evidence of how they interpret the events that took place, which perhaps could be regarded as bias or confirmation bias proper, a good example is in the evidence of [Dr B], when dealing with [Baby P] -- we have just touched on this in the interviews -- where she gave evidence that Lucy Letby had said something along the lines of, "He's not going to be leaving here", and that's plainly presented as something incriminatory in the way she gave that evidence. It wasn't disputed a comment like that might have been made, but of course the defence identified that might be a reasonable view given the concerns at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We submit that isolating details like that, or Lucy Letby smiling in the wrong way to the wrong person, are in themselves a good example of a tendency to construe against her her behaviour or events in the worst possible way or in an incriminatory fashion.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Allied to that is the second aspect of bias in this case or bearing upon or potentially bearing upon credibility, and that is the way some witnesses may have chosen to give evidence now or the way they've given evidence about Lucy Letby or things they've said that impact upon her.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Stephen Brearey has given evidence at various points, either specific to a count he's dealing with and occasionally more generally about concerns on the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Sometimes, we say, he has given evidence which is less helpful or deliberately unhelpful. I can give an illustration. When dealing with the case of [Baby G] and the question of whether bloody secretions had interfered with the breathing tube -- this may seem some while ago, but it's something I've considered after receiving this response.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Brearey discounted a bloody secretion could block an ETT. That's what he said. He questioned that, he questioned that in circumstances where we would say quite plainly we relied upon that as a possible explanation for a tube being blocked. And we would say he did that because he is biased against Lucy Letby and that affected the way in which he dealt with that question.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: To weigh up the merit or otherwise of our criticism of someone like Dr Brearey, material that shows that he was predisposed against her in some way or forming preconceived opinions is relevant. The two items that we identify that come from Eirian Powell's statement are examples of both of those. His direction or his expression to Eirian Powell at page 206, that he didn't want to include the doctors when considering who was present on the unit at the time of these events, is a preconception that colours the way in which he regards the evidence, we say.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And if that's his attitude there then it can't be dismissed from an attitude elsewhere in terms of preconceptions and taking the worst or a bad view, ultimately, of the defendant.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: More directly -- this is at the bottom of page 207 -- where Eirian Powell identified to Dr Brearey that there was at least one other nurse who, on her assessment, was the next most regularly present member of staff, and it's Nurse Melanie Taylor, at that point Dr Brearey said, "Oh yeah, but she's nice". Now, whether or not he ever said or ever described Lucy Letby as "Nice Lucy", which is something he said he'd said, or some complimentary term like that, and Eirian Powell doesn't suggest he did say that. But whether or not he ever did say that, what matters is that when he was presented with material about Lucy Letby alongside material about another nurse, in contradistinction to anything he said about Lucy Letby, he made the point of saying of Melanie Taylor, "Yeah, she's nice".
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We say that plainly discloses a bias against Lucy Letby on that evidence. It's powerful evidence of that. It's something we put to Dr Brearey, who dealt with it as he saw fit, but it's something that this witness can give evidence of. So this isn't a matter of going into questions of commonality more broadly, which was something that was raised as a concern by the prosecution originally, that somehow we were going to be inviting Eirian Powell to engage in her own analysis of who did what, where and when and how that dovetails with medical issues. It's a very discrete point but it's, we submit, a powerful illustration of a motivation or a bias against Lucy Letby. And when we make the criticisms of members of staff that we do, and we've criticised Dr Brearey, and we would do so, it is necessary for us to be able to call upon that. It has been put to him and we would wish to put it to Eirian Powell.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So it's a very limited matter but it's an important one so far as we're concerned and it indicates a hostility to Lucy Letby that is capable of affecting his attitude and the way he gives his evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: From that, my Lord, we move to points 5, 6, 7 and 8, which to some extent are different examples of a similar issue that develops over a period of time. Point 5 simply is questioning about the time that Lucy Letby was moved to day shifts in April 2016. When we say, as we do, that the prosecution raise this and the defence should be allowed to cross-examine upon it, it's a fact that's in evidence that in April 2016, or at some point, Ms Letby was moved to days. The prosecution have referred to that and we simply want to deal with why that happened, which is for the defendant's own benefit, we anticipate Eirian Powell would say, and deal simply with what happened there from --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, for her?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Of benefit because of the stresses of what had been taking place during other events at night.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right. Well, I don't know whether the jury have picked up, but there are a lot of incidents that take place in the early part of the indictment events here which take place during night shifts and then they happen during day shifts.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So anyway, I hear what you say, but I am not quite sure how far that's going to take you in any event.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: -- it can be relevant to both sides' cases.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's what happened. The jury know about it and since Eirian Powell explains why it happened, it may be something of help to have.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'll hear what the prosecution say in relation to that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Following on --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Non-clinical/clinical role in July 2016?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, this leads into points 7 and 8, which in large part no objection is taken to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: In July 2016, the fact is that Ms Letby was moved to a nonclinical role. blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And one at tile 263, signed by Eirian Powell and Eirian Powell's email and it described what has happened and how there's a review of competencies taking place.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: To deal with what lies behind that and the messages at that time and what was going on with the defendant and her position at that time, it's necessary and relevant, we say, for us to question Eirian Powell about that and the arrangements that were made for Lucy Letby to be moved from a clinical role and what she was told and how she reacted to it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Necessary and relevant, first of all, because this is in evidence from the prosecution already. blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: relevant because it feeds into a theme that is significant for the defence case, which is the impact of removal from the unit, increasing isolation and eventually, although this isn't for Eirian Powell, but eventually an awareness of blame in her direction for things that had taken place that led to a great deal of upset in the first instance and, the defence will maintain, mental anguish later on.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Not only is that relevant as part of the defendant's case, but it is also a relevant and necessary part of her case when we come to look at things that were written by her later on. There is a clear line, we submit, that follows from removal from the unit, how that happened, the grievance procedure, the details of which we do not seek to adduce, we are not, respectfully, interested in who said what about who at that point, it's the fact it took place. blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's a matter we have to resolve in some way, either by evidence or by agreed facts because that's a necessary part of the chronology.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Eirian Powell is a witness who deals with aspects of that in her statement and is able to give evidence on what happened, particularly in the move from the unit to a non-clinical role and the initial impact of that upon the defendant. That is what points 6, 7 and 8 relate to.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In point 8 we have gone into some detail to explain a matter that we would wish to raise with Eirian Powell about a meeting with Sian Williams in July 2017 in which what was happening was explained to the defendant, her reaction to that, and also what we say was the limited contact she was to have with certain people so she didn't feel more isolated than necessary.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Of course, their names and the contact with them is something that is a feature of what happens in the period that follows and this is relevant as to why they featured so heavily -- or at least relevant in part.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: And there may be competing interpretations of that, but that's the defence case on that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, on any view it's relevant. It's potentially relevant.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's potentially relevant. So that's what lies behind 6, 7 and 8.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Item 9, which is following matters relating to the grievance, insofar as Eirian Powell is able to deal with this we would want her to do so. It's not something we want to deal with at any extended length with her. If it tuns out that these matters can be agreed in some other formal fashion, then they can be. But some aspects of the agreed facts are still being settled. So at this point --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All right. I see what you're wanting there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, that's what we want.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Either by adducing it from the witness, you hope, or by way of agreed fact.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, my Lord. That's the position.

blocks.text: Thank you very much.

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, any fact that is necessary to be established that will ensure a fair trial of this defendant we will agree. So that's our basic position and technicalities aren't going to come in the way of that, just as they don't come in the way of the prosecution admitting relevant facts in any trial, even more so in a trial as serious as this one.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as our submissions about relevance are concerned, we identified what we submitted are the primary issues in the case. That wasn't intended to be an exhaustive list, but it's a fairly good touchstone, we would submit, in assessing where issues that are not so clear-cut -- or which side of the line issues that are not so clear-cut might fall.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The simple test to be applied is: evidence is admissible if it is relevant to an issue in the case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So one asks the question: to what issue is that evidence relevant?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: And if it is a matter that is in issue in the case, a bit like the Criminal Justice Act 2003 in deciding whether it's a matter of substantive value that's in issue between the prosecution and the defence, then it's admissible unless it's for some reason -- its prejudicial effect outweighs any probative value it may have. So really one just has to look at each individual piece of evidence and say: is that arguably relevant or not for one side or the other?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think we've narrowed this down quite considerably during --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You have and we have perhaps now narrowed it down even further.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: What the witness cannot do is express opinions about things. She can give evidence on the matters -- Mr Myers has helpfully accepted this -- about matters that are within her direct knowledge, but she can't go beyond that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So really, is all that's left the Dr Brearey...?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, I think the grievance is a fairly controversial area.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think it's the fact of a grievance procedure. It's difficult because it's in evidence in any event, isn't it? I think it's in evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I would have to check that, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We have -- actually, the final tile on the schedule, the post-indictment information, is the formal lodging of the grievance procedure on 7 September.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Exactly, so it's the extent to which one can go into the grievance procedure and the actual grievance procedure -- as I understand Mr Myers, the relevance, he says, is that it is potentially or it is relevant, say the defence, to material that is before the jury because some of that material was consequent upon there being a grievance procedure and what was taking place at that time.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then it just becomes, if that is right and if it's admissible, it's then the weight to be attached to it by the fact-finders.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And also the more vexed question and the one that's really going to cause problems or potential problems is to infer, as the defence are seeking to in the particular areas that they would like to establish, that the grievance was resolved in favour of Lucy Letby with all the consequential inferences that the jury might draw from that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Are you seeking that, Mr Myers? Is that what 9E is?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's the way -- we tried to put that as neutrally as possible because it's a fact that she was due to return to the unit and it's a fact that after that was going to take place, or before it could take place, the police were contacted. But that's the way that that goes. The investigation concluded in December 2016 and, after that was concluded, she was due to return in March 2017, which was as neutral a formulation as we could put for that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, no, because that carries huge implications, doesn't it? I mean, was her grievance upheld in the sense that there was no material upon which she could be prevented from returning to work?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It was upheld. We haven't gone into the detail.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: There's actually quite a lengthy report that upholds it.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: By whom?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not Eirian Powell.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not Eirian Powell, but moving away from Eirian Powell, as a fact of record it was upheld, and indeed -- and this isn't something we've gone close to -- the consultants were required to formally apologise to writing. We don't go to that, but we just make the point this isn't what we have tried to put in and we don't.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: This is a criminal trial based on the material that is now available. I hadn't appreciated that this point was going to be made and relied on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I hadn't read into 9E what you are now seeking to say.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But that is a very controversial issue that I am certainly not going to rule upon at this stage because I would be deeply unhappy to seek to adduce from a witness, who was not responsible for the conclusions of that grievance investigation, to give evidence about it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We understand that, which is why we include that because it's something we say is relevant. I hasten to add at no point have we sought, nor do we, to seek what happened at the conclusion of it or what happened with the consultants or what didn't happen with them. We're aware of that. But this matter, having been introduced, we observe, in just the same way the prosecution do, it has to be resolved in some way, otherwise it's just floating there with as much of a disadvantage to the defence as the prosecution perceive it has upon them, which is why we'd thought this was a neutral way of dealing with it. So that was why we thought this was something that she could deal with.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But we have a situation where the fact there was a grievance procedure is in evidence and just as much as the prosecution are anxious that that is not construed against their witnesses in any particular way, we have precisely the same concern that it isn't construed against the defendant, the outcome of that, because on one view it might be regarded that it was when we all know, whatever the basis for it, it was upheld in her favour. blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I can understand that. I'm just wondering whether there can't be the neutral fact that the grievance was lodged formally on 7 September 2016, there was a formal investigation into the grievance, it concluded in December 2016, and then the date when the police became involved -- just not giving any outcome in relation to it one way or the other.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Perhaps we can consider that, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That then gets the fact in because it gets the point in, which as I understood, you were urging, saying that this was preying on her mind, so to speak, that this was going on. Otherwise, if we go down the route of that and the thoroughness, the evidence, the material on which the grievance procedure was being determined...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We can see that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We've been spending, what, nearly 7 months going through the detailed evidence here, chart by chart, event by event. I'm not being critical of the grievance procedure, but I rather suspect it will be a sort of HR-driven process within the terms of the hospital management board, a completely different scenario.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. We don't perceive that in any way is going to resolve the key issues in this case, so we don't seek to use it in that way, but we do seek to ensure that the relevant chronology is there in some way.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have said what I have said and I am not going to say any more and I'm not adjudicating on it formally at this stage, but certainly, so far as that is concerned, I think it requires very careful thought so that it cannot be misconstrued. blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We can consider how best to deal with that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'll leave that with you. So it's just the Dr Brearey point. Otherwise I think that -- well, what I'll do is I'll put in writing what my conclusions are as to the extent to which these matters can be put in evidence.

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: there had only, in inverted commas -- I use that word only as a comparator to what was the position a year later (inaudible: no microphone).
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON
